title: Sweet Sellers Face Shelf-Life Labels for Loose Mithai Ahead of Diwali
excerpt: Uttar Pradesh and Uttarakhand now require use-by dates on unpackaged sweets — closing a disclosure gap, and adding per-batch compliance work for small halwais at peak season.
body:
• Uttar Pradesh requires every sweet displayed or stored for sale to carry a use-by date from October 15, 2026, including loose mithai sold from open trays, the state Food Safety and Drug Administration ordered.
  • Uttarakhand follows from October 26, requiring manufacturing and expiry dates to be displayed for unpackaged sweets and bakery products at the point of sale.
  • Shelf life varies by sweet — from one day to 30 days depending on ingredients and preparation — so each variety carries its own date, not a single shop-wide label.
  • For Diwali buyers: check the tray's use-by date before buying loose sweets; packaged sweets already carry expiry information, loose sweets historically did not.

Sweet sellers are heading into Diwali under a new compliance load: shelf-life dates for sweets that have never carried them. In Uttar Pradesh, the Food Safety and Drug Administration (FSDA) has ordered that from October 15, 2026, every sweet displayed or stored for sale must show a use-by date — explicitly covering loose, unpackaged mithai sold from open trays and counters, according to PTI reporting carried by LatestLY. Uttarakhand's Food Safety Commissioner Vinay Shankar Pandey has issued a parallel directive taking effect October 26, requiring manufacturing and expiry dates for unpackaged sweets and bakery products, NationPress reported.

Why loose sweets are the target

Packaged sweets already carry expiry information. Loose sweets did not, and inspections found consumers could not determine when a sweet was prepared or how long it remained safe to eat. The gap matters most at Diwali, when purchases and gifting surge and shops produce in volume. The FSDA noted that usable periods vary widely — roughly one day to 30 days depending on the sweet's ingredients, preparation and storage — so the date must reflect the individual product, not a blanket period. The UP order sits under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, and inspectors will now check disclosure, not just product condition and premises.

"For Diwali buyers: check the tray's use-by date before buying loose sweets; packaged sweets already carry expiry information, loose sweets historically did not."

The burden on small sellers

For small halwais, the work is real. Loose sweets are made in small batches and replenished multiple times a day, so tracking and labelling shelf life per batch adds administrative work and compliance cost at the highest-volume moment of the year, Whalesbook's industry analysis noted — on top of elevated prices for milk, sugar, edible oils and dry fruits that already squeeze margins. Larger organised brands, with automated tracking and laboratory testing in place, absorb the same rules more easily, a shift analysts say could accelerate share moving from unorganised to branded sellers. In a separate UP measure, the FSDA has also prohibited ethylene glycol and diethylene glycol as coolants in milk and dairy processing units.

What buyers should do

The rule hands the shopper a simple check: before buying loose mithai for Diwali, look for the use-by date on the tray or counter for that specific variety, and ask the seller if it is not displayed — from October 15 in Uttar Pradesh and October 26 in Uttarakhand, display is mandatory. For diaspora readers ordering festival sweets through family back home or importing packaged brands, the distinction holds: packaged products already carry dates; it is the open-tray purchase, the Diwali staple, that these orders finally bring into the same disclosure standard.
